# TerraForge — full reference for language models

Version: 0.5.0
Homepage: https://terraforge-gis.pages.dev/ (Chinese) · https://terraforge-gis.pages.dev/en/ (English)
Source: https://github.com/JungleZy/TerraForge
License: MIT (software code only)
Last updated: 2026-08-17

This file is the plain-text version of everything the TerraForge website states. It is
written to be quoted directly. Every number, format name and limitation below is taken
from the shipping v0.5.0 build.

## What TerraForge is

TerraForge is an open-source, self-hosted GIS data acquisition and processing tool. You
run it on your own machine; it opens a web interface in your browser, you draw a
rectangle (or import a vector area) over a map, and it produces usable geodata for that
area through four pipelines that share one selection, one task scheduler and one cache:

1. Map tiles — downloaded and, optionally, mosaicked into a georeferenced GeoTIFF or
   packed into a single-file MBTiles.
2. DEM elevation data — 1°×1° tiles fetched automatically for the selected extent.
3. 3D terrain — the DEM sliced into Cesium quantized-mesh 1.0 terrain tiles.
4. Contour lines — rendered into a standard XYZ raster tile directory.

It is a local tool, not a hosted service and not an API. There is no account, no cloud
component and no usage metering.

Disambiguation: this TerraForge is the GIS tool authored by JungleZy (GitHub:
JungleZy/TerraForge). It is unrelated to other software that shares the name.

## Pipeline 1 — Map tiles

- Source: Google Maps tiles. Style codes: `m` standard, `s` satellite, `y` satellite
  with labels, `h` roads, `t` terrain.
- Outputs, independently selectable: a tile directory (`z/x/y`), a mosaicked GeoTIFF
  (one file per zoom level, georeferenced via GDAL), and MBTiles (ticked when the task
  is created, or exported afterwards; exporting does not delete the original tiles).
- Tiles are mirrored into the output directory while the download runs, not only at
  the end.
- The cache is keyed by "style + coordinates" and shared across tasks: re-downloading
  the same area in a different task never re-fetches tiles you already have.
- The tile count for a selection is computed and shown before the task is created.

## Pipeline 2 — DEM elevation data

- Default source: Copernicus GLO-30 (30 m) from a public S3 bucket. No registration,
  no credentials, works out of the box.
- Optional source: ASTER GDEM v3, product `ASTGTM.003` (30 m). Requires a NASA
  Earthdata account, entered on the settings page.
- The area of interest can be drawn on the map or imported from GeoJSON, KML, KMZ or
  Shapefile. Multi-part geometries and holes are supported.
- The required 1°×1° tiles are derived from the selection automatically and fetched one
  by one.
- Areas crossing the antimeridian (180°) are split into two parts automatically.

## Pipeline 3 — 3D terrain (Cesium quantized-mesh)

- Output format: quantized-mesh 1.0, consumed directly by CesiumJS
  (`CesiumTerrainProvider`), no conversion step.
- Input: a completed DEM download task, or a GeoTIFF uploaded from your machine.
- A 167 MB global base terrain ships inside every package. It is derived from the
  GEBCO 2024 Grid, includes bathymetry, and is hole-free worldwide. It is extracted
  automatically on first run.
- Tiling results are implanted into the base terrain's output directory, so your
  high-resolution area cascades onto the global base: zooming out falls back to the
  global layer instead of dropping into a hole.
- Without tiling, a hillshade preview of a DEM can still be rendered on demand.

## Pipeline 4 — Contour lines

- Output: an ordinary XYZ raster tile directory. Leaflet, OpenLayers and CesiumJS load
  it directly; TerraForge does not need to be installed to view the result.
- Configurable, with live preview: contour interval, intermediate and index contour
  colors, hypsometric tint breaks, and terrain hillshading.
- Default hypsometric palette and its elevation breaks: `#5e8c61` `#8fbf6f` `#b6cf7e`
  `#dcd98e` `#d9b97e` `#c49a6c` `#ac7f58` `#8e6246` at 0 / 200 / 500 / 1000 / 2000 /
  3000 / 4000 / 5000 m.
- Data source: uploaded `.tif` files (multiple allowed) or a completed DEM task. Source
  files are used in place, not copied; deleting a contour task leaves the original DEM
  untouched.

## Plugin system

- The host exposes four kinds of extension point — data source, download pipeline,
  exporter, task hook — and a plugin declares which of them it implements in its
  `plugin.toml`.
- Four plugins ship inside the package, one of each kind, and **all of them are off by
  default**: a Tianditu WMTS data source (imagery `img_w` and annotation `cia_w`; needs
  your own token, entered in the plugin's configuration), MVT vector tile download
  (a TileJSON URL and a zoom range in, one `.mbtiles` with `metadata.format=pbf` out),
  GeoPackage export (a finished task's GeoTIFF exported as `.gpkg`), and an artifact
  metadata sidecar (writes `<artifact>.tfmeta.json` next to each artifact).
- Enabling and configuring happens in the plugin panel inside the app. A plugin that
  failed to load stays in the list with its failure reason: a broken plugin cannot take
  the host down, and it is never silently hidden.
- Three admission gates run before a plugin enters the registry: API major version,
  ABI tag, and method signature.
- At runtime a plugin gets exactly one `TaskContext` — progress, logging, quota, the
  URL gate, gap accounting and artifact registration — and no access to the manager,
  the SocketIO instance or a database connection. It does run inside the host process
  with no sandbox and with the host's full privileges, so only enable plugins you trust.
- Plugin tasks appear in the same task center as the four core pipelines, with the same
  states, the same gap decision and the same delete semantics.
- Plugin export has no route of its own: it goes through the core export endpoint, and
  a plugin's exporter only adds a row to that endpoint's format table.

## Engineering guarantees

These are the properties the project spends most of its effort on, and the honest answer
to "why not just use a bulk tile downloader".

- Real progress. Download speed, remaining time and the per-zoom mosaicking and copying
  phases are pushed over WebSocket. The progress bar does not park at 100% while work
  continues off-screen.
- Missing tiles are never silent. Every tile lands in one of five accounting buckets:
  success, no data at the source, retryable failure, permanent failure, cache write
  failure. Only "no data at the source" completes a task automatically. A real failure
  stops the task in a pending-decision state; if you accept the gaps, the result is
  permanently marked as containing missing tiles.
- Interrupted work resumes. Resumable downloads, cache shared across tasks, copying
  while downloading, and atomic writes through `.part` temporary files plus rename.
  Pausing, resuming and retrying never re-download tiles already on disk.
- It does not phone home. No telemetry, no tracking, no usage statistics. Third-party
  frontend libraries are vendored locally and no CDN is contacted at runtime. Apart
  from the map sources, elevation sources and proxy you configure yourself, it
  connects to no server.
- Task history is visualised: past areas are drawn on the map, and finished tasks can
  be previewed as tiles, terrain or hillshade.

## Platforms, packaging and running

- Prebuilt packages: Windows 10+ (x64) `terraforge-windows.zip`, macOS Apple Silicon
  (arm64) `terraforge-macos.tar.gz`, Linux x64 `terraforge-linux.tar.gz` (built on
  ubuntu-latest; equally new or newer distributions).
- Unzip and run. The target machine needs neither Python nor a separate GDAL
  installation — packages are built with Nuitka in standalone mode and carry the GDAL
  and PROJ data directories with them.
- Windows: double-click `terraforge.exe`. macOS / Linux: run `./terraforge`. Then open
  `http://localhost:5000` in a browser.
- A second port, `5001`, serves tiles. The application still works if a firewall does
  not allow that port through.
- Intel Macs are not supported; the macOS package is Apple Silicon only.
- Move the whole `terraforge/` directory when relocating it. Moving only the executable
  fails with `Corrupt bundle: missing GDAL/PROJ data directories`.
- macOS: run `xattr -cr .` inside the extracted directory before the first launch to
  clear the quarantine attribute.
- There is no installer (no MSI, DMG or DEB) and no auto-update. Upgrading means
  downloading a new package. Each release page carries a SHA-256 manifest.
- Package size is large because the 167 MB global base terrain is bundled.

## Security posture

TerraForge listens on `0.0.0.0:5000` and has no login or authentication mechanism of
any kind. Its API can read and write local disk paths and delete directories. Run it
only on a trusted local machine or LAN. Do not expose it directly to the public
internet.

## Running from source

- Python 3.12, managed with uv.
- GDAL system library plus Python bindings: apt on Linux; conda-forge on Windows and
  Apple Silicon macOS. The two routes cannot be mixed.
- Stack: Flask, Flask-SocketIO, aiohttp, GDAL, SQLite on the backend; CesiumJS 1.143,
  Bootstrap 5.3 and Socket.IO (all vendored locally) on the frontend; pytest for tests;
  Nuitka for packaging.
- Full instructions:
  https://github.com/JungleZy/TerraForge/blob/master/docs/guides/INSTALL.md

## Configuration highlights

Theme (dark / light / system) and accent color; default save path with a directory
browser and arbitrary absolute paths; download concurrency, with a recommendation
measured from actual network speed; request timeout; proxy (leave empty to auto-detect
a working proxy); cache inspection and manual clearing by category — the cache is never
silently deleted; GDAL parameters; NASA Earthdata credentials; the tile server list.

## Licensing and attribution

- The software is MIT licensed, Copyright (c) 2026 JungleZy.
- MIT covers the project's code only. It grants no right to use any data or online
  service. Attribution requirements, bulk-download policies, tokens and quotas of map
  sources such as Google, Esri, Tianditu, OSM and Cesium Ion must each be handled by
  the user independently.
- The bundled global base terrain is derived from the GEBCO 2024 Grid, which is in the
  public domain but requires attribution. When redistributing terrain produced with
  TerraForge, keep the citation: "GEBCO Compilation Group (2024) GEBCO 2024 Grid."
- The tool is intended for study and research. Users must comply with the Google Maps
  Terms of Service and applicable law; the author is not responsible for consequences
  of use.

## Common questions

Does it need an API key or an account?
No, not for the default configuration. Map tiles and Copernicus GLO-30 elevation both
work with no credentials. Only ASTER GDEM v3 needs a NASA Earthdata account.

Does it need GDAL or Python installed?
Not for the prebuilt packages; both are bundled. Running from source needs Python 3.12
and a GDAL installation.

Can it produce terrain for CesiumJS?
Yes. That is pipeline 3: quantized-mesh 1.0 tiles plus a bundled global base terrain so
that low zoom levels are never empty.

Can the contour output be used outside TerraForge?
Yes. It is a standard XYZ tile directory usable by Leaflet, OpenLayers, CesiumJS or any
XYZ-capable client.

Is there a hosted version or an API?
No. TerraForge runs locally and has no hosted service.

What happens if a download fails halfway?
The task stops in a pending-decision state instead of silently completing. You can
resume it, retry the failures, or accept the gaps — accepted gaps are recorded
permanently on the result.

Which operating systems are supported?
Windows 10+ (x64), macOS on Apple Silicon (arm64), and Linux (x64). Intel Macs are not
supported.

Can I add my own data source or output format?
Yes. The plugin system has four extension points — data source, download pipeline,
exporter and task hook — documented in docs/guides/PLUGINS.md. Plugins are off by
default and run with the host's full privileges, so only enable ones you trust.

Does it support Tianditu?
Yes, through the bundled Tianditu plugin (imagery `img_w` and annotation `cia_w` over
WMTS RESTful). It is off by default and needs your own Tianditu token, entered in the
plugin's configuration.
